changes.summary: Tony Cokes works with appropriated text from various sources, including popular music, mass media, and historical and theoretical writing, and remixes it into video, signs, lightboxes, and billboards. Composed of vibrant colors and often set to music, Cokes’s work subverts the language that shapes contemporary life and culture to draw out new meanings and sensations. For his first public outdoor presentation in Chicago, Cokes presents a two-part installation on the Art Institute’s Bluhm Family Terrace. The terrace windows facing Millennium Park become a billboard—viewable from across the street and the park below—with the phrase “Let yourself be free,” drawn from Aretha Franklin’s 1968 recording of “Think.” Franklin frequently visited and sang in Chicago with her father, a prominent pastor and civil rights leader, and it was here that she earned her lifelong title, the Queen of Soul, originally coined by Chicago DJ Pervis Spann at the Regal Theater in Bronzeville in May 1964. The presentation also includes one of Cokes’s freestanding signs, reading “We don’t have the freedom to be bored anymore,” and “There’s a set of forces that want us to be permanently anxious.” Both sentences are from the English cultural theorist Mark Fisher. Together, they question the meaning of freedom in a present defined by rapid technological change and the erosion of private life.
